Name: Steve Heckman
Question: What should I do if I failed two college classes?
Answer: Being that there are a number of excellent answer out there already, I thought I’d appeach this by adding two points. First, sometimes we stretch ourselves. After all, you are not really learning anything if it takes no effort. But in this case, you should think carefully if you are adding an extra class or several classes that have a reputation for being difficult. Now, some majors have a required course load that you can do little about, unless you opt for a light course load that has you extending your time in college (which can be expensive!) Think Engineering or Physics. The math alone is fairly intense. The second factor is that should not have occured out of the blue! You should have know early on that these two courses were starting to get out of hand. On the plus side, when you retake the classes, you have already been through both once already, so at least its not completely new material. And you also have some idea what aspect were hard for you, so you can focus on these areas.

Name: Steve Heckman
Question: What is the average failure rate for college classes taught by instructors?
Answer: When researching this answer, this was one of my first responses… Generally, tenured professors have the “best” pass rate, as they have significant experience, and a lighter course load. Once you taught a course a few times, you tend to learn what works well, and make adjustments to earlier material that students had a difficult time with. Teaching Assistants (often gard students) have the worst outcomes, which again is logical. They, after all, would be teaching only for a short time and then move on. Moreover, they would have little practical experience outside school, and at best its limited to internships. Instructors (Non-tenure-track instructors or lecturers) fall somewhere in between. Some are fulltime and can build up both experience, and refine their courses over time to improve outcomes. I have taught in the past, and the hardest class to teach is always the first one of any subject. Your lessons plans get refined, as was as the exams. Of course, you still need to meet the college requirements, but I found you have lots of leeway to make that class your own. I’ve started teaching again (this is my first semester returning) in our community college’s mechatronics program. So I’m going to be living the “first class syndrome” yet again, but i also to take this in account. Fortunately it’s a “lab course” so the majority of the grade will come from both lab assignments and their project (some 75%).

Name: Steve Heckman
Question: Is sales engineer a good job?
Answer: Look, as an engineer I normally make fun of sales but at the end of the day, it is an vital part of the organization. After all, its role is to bring the company (and by extension, the engineering staff) new project & customers. Without them we would have no work, and thus we would be poor! Now, this is also an aspect to consider that most do not, in that we have two types of sales. Most people think of business to customer sales, as that is what they see everyday. From sales associates at the Buy More, used car sales or even real estate agents, they think of someone selling one on one. But business to business is completely different, in the sense that almost everyone is different. In most cases you are trying to create a long-term relationship. And keep in mind that sales engineers are engineers. In our company 100% of the sales engineers have engineering degrees. Now, they are not “designing” or problems solving in the traditional sense. But what they are doing is showing how their companies product can solve their customer’s problems. In one company I worked for, the sale engineers were closer to “applications engineers” in that they would design communication systems for prospects using all of the components we made. The other aspect is that many sales engineers get to travel. Each of our SE’s travel to visit customers once a quarter, which is not excessive. And we have one flagship trade show (MD&M West) what is in Anaheim, Ca which is quite the perk being we are on the east coast. But like I said, it can also be employer specific, as one company could be a dysfunctional pressure cooker and down the street the same role could be a dream job!

Question: My college is getting closed and I have not completed my degree. They are forcing me to transfer to another college. What can I do?
Answer: So, the school is closing. You having a bake sale to help save it is not going to help. In a sense they are not forcing you to transfer to another college, circumstances are. I’m pretty sure they dont want to close, after all. In you case, I’d advise transfering. You goal is to get another degree. And they might have worked out an articulation agreement with that other college in order to maximise the credits you transfer (most schools do require a minimum residency requirement in order to earn a degree, so be aware of that). Look, I get that you picked your present school over the other option available, and not being able to graduate stings to a large degree. But you need to move forward and adapt to changing circumstances. Again, this is a less than optimum situation to be in. How you deal with it is an indication of how you will deal with problems later in life.

Question: Is it necessary for engineers to study physics and chemistry before entering their field in order to have a scientific understanding of how things work?
Answer: I believe so. Keep in mind that at the end of the day, engineering is essentially applied physics. So learning about physics formally, even if you major (branch) of engineering is just a subset of overall physics. Moreover, when one is designing or troubleshooting, there may be factors involved that fall outside your normal area of expertise. There also may be some overlap. As a manufacturing engineer, I tend to pull from all branches of engineering. I’ve used CAD to design fixtures, designed test systems (including writing the code), had to learn PCB design, use lean six sigma (statistics) to solve problems. I also had to learn material properties (steels, plastics), adhesive chemistries and electroplating basics. In one case I toured a local test lab, where they used the scanning electron microscope to determine why solder joints were failing (we found that the solder used was not RoHS, when it should have been. Thus, the presence of excess lead was interacting with the gold plating and causing a weak solder connection. In this case, I did not have to perform the test, but I had to 1) know it was an option and 2) understand the implication of the results. The greatest benefit of studying science is being immersed in the scientific method itself. You will be solving problems as much as designing new things, so having a good background in root cause analysis is very important. But I also made this point: engineering is a creative endeavor, no less than art. But unlike art, you are imposed various rules by the universe itself! After all, ohm's law is not a suggestion, nor are the laws of thermodynamics. And in addition, one other principle stands out: the more you know, the more creative you can be! A lot of design is synthesis, in that you might combine two existing things in a new way no one has considered before. But you had to know both things existed before you could do that! So, yes, the science track that engineers learn in school has tremendous value.

Question: I am now back in this hellhole called school, how do I get out of here?
Answer: Graduate! In my case, I loved learning but hated school with the force of a thousand suns. Most of it was because i was a nerd that never really fit in. Almost three decades later, I ran into this article by Paul Graham, that finally help me understand what in the hell was going on… Now, there were a few things that help me to survive, maybe some of these can help, or you will need to find your own. First, I still enjoyed many of my classes. Again, for me the hell was not so much the subjects, but the feeling if you did too well you got bullied to a degree. Second, I got a part-time “after school” job where I primarily worked with adults. They accepted me, and I felt like I fit in. Paychecks were a big bonus. Third, in my case those paychecks allowed me to purchase my first car. Having mobility means that I had some control over my social life. I also embraced doing some things alone. At least once a week I stopped by a pizza place on my way to work, and often sat there and read a book while eating a few slices. But it was never on Thursdays, as that was meatball sub might with my work crew. Four, I also read a lot. Being in your own world helps! Five, my one concession to coolness was going to the Rocky Horror Picture Show. Looking back, skiting was big in the 70’s when I grew up. I should have showed up more. Now, in my case once I graduated, I first enlisted in the USAF (which allowed me to reinvent myself) and then I took night courses until I earned my degree. I also picked an Airforce career with one of the longest tech schools. I knew this was not going to be a repeat of high school, as in most states the drink age was still 18. And about college, I need to make this point: Most people want to be there (as opposed to high school) and are actually interested in their major. Plus, in college being smart is a “plus” (or at was in the past). But night courses have the additional bonus of having more adult students, many who are looking to finish their degree, or get one to improve job prospects. They take school seriously and have more interesting stories than just kids your own age. So don't let high school turn you off from going to college (or a trade school).

Name: Steve Heckman
Question: How can we see the Milky Way Galaxy and be inside it at the same time?
Answer: Remember we are only seeing part of it. Think of it as being in a house where you can only see the room you are in. You are still “seeing” that house, but the view to the rest is blocked. But if you look out a window, you can see other houses just fine. All of the individual stars are still part of that same disk. They are just closer to us.

Question: Is the left going to eliminate higher education due to the lack of education in public schools, making it so kids are far less likely to be college material?
Answer: No. At worst, they are just going to continue to lower standards to meet DEI goals. There are two reasons for this: Look, the right tends to shoot itself in the foot on this one as well, but just a different foot. Ask my good friend Prottay, he does make a few excellent points about how conservatives avoid college because they are afraid its Uncle Charlie’s Summer camp. Its not all or nothing here. I believe both sides fail to see the larger picture. College does teach useful skills, including logical & critical thinking, communication skills as well a prepare students for specific careers. You are not going to be a CPA nor an engineer without education. Another point: college has been watered down to a degree because we have so many average students attending. It unavoidable as we send nearly 50% of all female high school students and 40% of all male. Now they might benefit from more schooling, no one can argue against that. But what is the cost-benefit ratio? And as for alternatives, I'm speaking on online programs like edX or coursera. Or making night school more mainstream. As in maybe attend for two years and get an associates degree and employment, and then finish a BA or BS degree as a part-time student. I’m not suggesting we do this 100%, but it should be a major option that is officially promoted, to the point where half would use this option. One benefit is the students are now in the “real world” as well as being a student. That was one advantage I had. It took 10 years to complete a degree, but it was also a 10-year internship where I had a chance to apply what i was learning.

In other words, I would suggest a good engineer is an average engineer, in the context that someone who is an engineer is already smarter than average and is quite capable. In case you want to be better than average…. Now, let define a better person! That of course is very elusive, as we could have as many opinions on how to become better as we have people! Question: Do students typically get higher grades in electives or in their major courses? Choosing electives (& fulfilling general education/core requirements) do students gravitate toward more leniently- or tougher-graded options? Do career goals affect this?
Answer: This is another question where the answer is “it depends” For engineering students, in many cases electives are seen as an easy “A” or a break from their core courses. That is not to say that they dont like their major, far from it. Its just that its a lot of hard work, and sometimes its fun to take something easier that is just fun. But I can also see why people might stretch themselves or explore a new option. But keep in mind that if you made significant progress, that do-overs are expensive.

Name: Steve Heckman
Question: When applying for engineering jobs, which is more important on a CV: education or work experience?
Answer: This is one of those questions that has been around for ages and is not limited to engineering. But in this case, you do have one factor to consider, that that an engineering degree is more or less the ticket to an engineering role in the first place. Now, keep in mind when applying for your first job out of college, you have very little experience, as you are looking for a true entry-level role where you are largely competing with other new graduates. Now, if out of school for a number of years, then your experience (and accomplishments) starts to matter way more. All of your competition will have a degree, as I said earlier it's an expected “baseline.” So now showcase what you have done with that degree! To conclude by repeating myself: It depends on where you are in your career, but after 2–3 years' experience starts to become more important, and the degree is just a “checkbox” item.

Question: Will you be called a “two-degree” holder if you finished two associate degrees that are completely different in the field?
Answer: In the US, the baseline for having a college degree in formal conversation is a bachelor’s degree. Now, I have seem people hold dual degrees, and I guess you could call them a “two-degree holder.” But the vast majority of people go on to earn a master’s degree, as opposed to a second bachelor's. Now, where do associates degrees fit into all of this? Well, first a community college is still college, but an associate's degree is only half a bachelor's degree. And, no, two associates' degree do not equal a bachelors, even if you pass 120 semester hours! In addition, they come in two flavors: Applied science or arts degrees are designed for sending a graduate straight to work. It is possible to continue and earn a bachelor's degree, but your options are limited. An associate’s in science is designed for transfer, and is essentially duplicating the first two years of a states bachelors degree program.

Name: Steve Heckman
Question: When can we expect to see price drops in electronics? Why have prices not been decreasing as they used to?
Answer: There were several reasons that we saw prices fall in the past, as well as why we saw price increase recently. First, all new technology is more expensive at first. Part of that is the manufacturing processes as well as the part designs are still being refined. (Radio Manufacturing in 1928) More manual assembly Modern SMT manufacturing So, in many areas we hit a wall where improvements are not as dramatic as when some of these major improvements were first introduced. But that is the technological forces driving down costs, we also have economic factors. First is basic supply & demand. As many have pointed out, covid was the 800-pound gorilla in causing out supply chain issues. Pretty much everything shutdown in 2020, and when it came back you not only had your normal demand as before, but you were also behind in many areas. So, when you are behind, suppliers have 0% incentive to off discounts or lower prices, as you already can't keep up with demand. Second, many manufacturers have chased after low-cost countries to keep costs low. Domestic US and European manufacturers could not keep up with workers in China making less than 1/10th of their wages. However, costs have gone up in these countries, and there are few remaining cheaper places to go to that have the workforces that could compete, or at the scale that would make a difference. Last, rising tariffs and energy prices have also increase costs, in areas that manufacturers can do nothing about. Perhaps we have driven out as much cost as we really need to, and should instead focus on value, performance and sustainability.

Question: What are some alternative solutions to storing solar power for nighttime use besides batteries?
Answer: For personal systems (ie, home) you really dont have many options. The best you can do is “sell” energy to the utility during peak production and then buy it back during the nighttime. Now, at the utility level, they do have more options. My favorite is pumped storage hydropower. While some systems are simply a set of reservoirs (closed-loop), where water is pumped to the higher reservoir during the day, and is released back to the lower reservoir in the evening. But those fed by a stream/river (open-loop) have the advantage of having that stream provide energy as well, that could make up for the pumping losses. Image source: pumped-storage-hydropower From the same link we learn that “PSH currently accounts for 96% of all utility-scale energy storage in the United States.” One local example was Smith Mountain Lake Dam, on the Roanoke River. Its capacity is 560 MW, not counting the Leesville dams' hydropower turbine output. Given the pumped storage hydropower systems are already at 96%, and it appears that batteries are a significant part of the remaining 4% and growing as well, that does not leave too many other alternatives as this time. One alternative was the “gravity battery” were a crane erects a ring of blocks to store energy to be released later. It does have the advantage of suitable for nearly any site, so they could be placed in cities, or at the source of production, or anywhere in between. I have no idea how stable they are in heavy winds, so that might need to be addressed.

Question: What are the potential disadvantages of using higher voltages than normal household electricity? Should households consider using voltages higher than 110 volts?

Now, the major disadvantage in using 220vac in North America is virtually all appliances require 110. So you would be quite limited in what you can purchase. Now, I have owned TVs that were 110–220 and even had a travel hairdryer, but again in many cases the selection is quite limited in retail stores. In addition, all you outlets would need to be brought up to code. The US does have an official outlet for 220… (image from Amazon) This would be a NEMA Receptacle Configuration 6-20R. But how many clock radios come with that plug attached? I’ve seen people who have also mounted a european outlet in their kitchen to use 220-based appliances, but I’m not sure if that would be to code. Again, that limits shopping to online suppliers and that would probably include overseas shipping. Note, this person (reddit) installed a proper outlet so he could use a UK tea kettle. Also note the white adapter. He could have also just cut off the plug and installed a new one. So the largest disadvantage is inconvenience. Now, some might bring up safety, as you are doubling the voltage. But the fact is we don’t find 10% of the EU population dead each year from electrocution, so it's probably not an issue.

For example, too much might also allow excessive current as Xc goes down with an increase in capacitance. You might ended up with the motor overheating. That said, you must use a equal or higher voltage rating. The only side effect of a higher voltage rating is it might be larger in size. Never, ever use a lower voltage rated component. Question: Is it true that every wire carries current?
Answer: In general, no. In a two-conductor lamp cord, of course both conductors carry the same current. The same would be true in a simple battery circuit. But real life is not limited to simple 2-wire systems. In most homes, you have hot, neutral and ground wires. The hot and neutral under ideal conditions carry the same current. The ground wire should have no current at all unless we have a failure. Now, in a 3-phase system the neutral conductor will not carry current if all three phases are balanced. Now, that might be true in a piece of equipment with just a 3-phase motor or power supply. But in a building, where lighting might be distributed across all three phases, it would be hard to ensure 100% balance takes place. All someone needs to do is turn off the lights in one room… Last, we also have situations where we have multiconductor cables. Some supply power, others carry discrete signals, and yet others carry data. At any specific time only a few of the conductors would be actively carrying current, so again the answer is no. I found at time just trying to come up with an idea for the paper was the hardest part. Now, there are other things to consider: you could take a class or two during the summer semester. Especially if its online and it allows you to still take an intern job. Two classes at a time (for four summer semesters) are more or less eight courses, or 24 semester hours. Of course, you need to consider it not free, including room & board, so if you live at home during the summer that needs to be considered. But if you are able to graduate a semester earlier than your classmates, you might have an advantage in looking for a position (of course, you are also completing with people who graduated a year earlier) It might also benefit the most those students looking for a dual degree, as remember there is a concept called “opportunity cost” The last and most importing thing to consider: Can you handle an extra course each semester without it negatively affecting your performance? Many take only four and add a year to their stay (not entirely uncommon with engineering) so trying to do the opposite might have a big negative impact on your GPA.

Question: Is it common for students who do poorly in high school to have successful careers?
Answer: The first thing we need to do is define what success look like. Is it based on employment? Are only doctors, lawyers, engineers, accountants and managers considered successful? Or do we include people who are plumbers & electricians, auto mechanics, police & fireman, and all of the other careers that don't require a degree also a success? So, someone who didn't do well in school could enlist in the Army, and later find a job as a heavy equipment operator in the construction industry. The reason I point this out is many people consider college to be the only path to success, and then define success only in terms of having a college-major related career. I challenge those who feel that way to open up their criterial for success, as many people pursuing that path often make more money than someone with a BA in Art History. But here’s the thing: it's possible for people who have done poorly in high school to also go on to college and earn a degree. Community colleges offer many a “second chance” academically. Yes, you may need to start out with remedial courses, but once past that you are still in a college that allows you to continue on more or less on the same path as anyone else going to college. In my case, I used a community college because one was “outside the main gate” at my first USAF assignment. Finally, we need to assess the reason someone didn't do well in high school. Was it the school (kid) culture? In my case I had honor roll years, and others where I barely passed (8th and 11th grades). A lot of that was due to feeling that I didn't fit in. I loved to learn, and was constantly reading. I like my teachers as well, I just hated “school” with enough energy to power the average home. I much later found out why: There are of course other factors as well: In my case the solution was to move (like i said, though by and large I hated high school, the USAF had its own community college, so I spent the next 10 years taking classes until I had started graduate classes.) Nevertheless, if each class had pizza I might have been happier!

Question: Can an employer legally record conversations with employees using personal devices (land line or cell)?
Answer: This depends on the state you live in (US-centric answer). In Virginia, eighter parts can legally record a conversation that they are part of. What you cannot do is connect a recorder and leave it on unintended, as that is considered wiretapping. What was interesting is I worked for a company that designed paging systems, and one of the interesting features was a “talk back” option. If you paged an office for example, it essentially became a speakerphone (or intercom). But we also have a tone alert switch, which produced “beep” to alert people that the speaker-mic was now active. That again preventing the boss from listening to break-room chatter. Now, keep in mind that company owned devices still fall under these rules, but they also have a fight to see what activates goes on (read email, review call log) so while it's not eavesdropping, it can still be incriminating if you are misusing company property. But they only have the right to review devices like phones for confidential information. Of course, give the size of micro-SD cards, good luck with that if someone is that determined to risk prison time.

Question: Can a termination be changed to a resignation after you have been terminated?
Answer: This really hits into a gray area, as once you were terminated (fired) you are no longer an employee, so the records would have to be modified after the fact. In many cases a company will pressure you to resign as opposed to being fired, as it helps to keep their unemployment “insurance” rates lower (in the US). If you resign (again with exceptions) you typically don't get unemployment compensation, so now you have no income for months when trying to find a job. It would seem that trying to classify this into a resignation after the fact means that someone in the organization made a serious error, as most of the time they wish you well while hoping to never see you again. The only scenario where people accept resigning vs being fired is when they did something quasi-illegal themselves (dishonest on travel vouchers or PTO) or even illegal (stealing). In this case it might be “quit or we’ll press charges. Ironically, I write this less than 24 hours after our QA manager was let go. Name: Steve Heckman
Question: Which is more correct, the Dilbert Principle or the Peter Principle?
Answer: The Peter Principle is far more common. Keep in mind that the Peter Principle recognizes that competent workers are promoted until they finally reach their level of incompetence. The reason for this is that management roles require new skills from the job they had done earlier. The Dilbert Principle promotes people to positions to where they will do the least harm. But this can be successful only in a few limited circumstances. Our company sees areas like our stock room to be a promotion over rank & file production workers, so some who does poorly at assembly might do ok kitting jobs. But to intention promote someone who is poor at their job, as opposed to just letting them go is something that only offers in limited circumstances: family businesses or the person was a real brown-noser. Or they were well liked to the point their manager wants to find something they could do. Another reason I’m going with the Peter Principle is many companies have a promote from within policy. They literally need to take a very good workers and place them in a job they may not be prepared for. Now, sometimes they do well, as if this had a 100% failure rate no one would do it. Even with highly educated worker like engineers, promotions to management roles can be risky, as like I said, there are part of management (dealing with personal conflicts, staffing including firing) that goes beyond just being “analytical” And here’s another thing to consider: each level of managing is very different. First-line supervisors have to deal with personal problems firsthand (workers are late, conflicts between workers) whereas mid-managers start managing supervisors or lower-level managers. So, you now are dealing with people who are already a cut above, but you focus is more on planning. Senior managers have to think strategically, which again is another new skill than most people don't have.

Name: Steve Heckman
Question: I was fired 3 days ago out of nowhere after 5 years. Now, the CEO emails me that my job has been “re-instated”, but when I come back, I will get a warning for “low performance”. What can I do?
Answer: I agree with many of the other answers here, in that something has occurred outside of the ordinary behind the scenes. First, its exceptionally rare for a company to admit a mistake, even as a half hearted attempt that seems to be going on. Second, make sure you have already fired for unemployment. In many places the window of opportunity is small. Third, I would play along for a while (while looking for another job) and ask about that low performance thing. I would require an explanation (maybe even see it in writing) I would not go back if I was me, for the same reason I would not accept a counteroffer when giving notice. You never know just how much resentment is actually simmering under the hood.

Question: How would you explain the Dilbert Principle to someone who’s never heard of it before?
Answer: First, we need to make sure they know of the earlier Peter Principle, as they are related but have one major difference. As for the Peter Principle, it's based on the premise that most organizations will reward their best workers with promotions into a supervisory role. But there the kicker, while some companies have working supervisors (at the lowest management level) many do not. In other words, you took you best mechanic and made them your shop manager. Now, they will better understand the day-to-day issues mechanics experience, or even help someone solve a problem. But they could really suck at the management part of the job. So, according to the Peter Principle, most to rise up to the level where they become incompetent and remain there. The Dilbert principle takes this a step farther: companies tend to promote incompetent employees to management to minimize their ability to harm productivity. So, the Peter Principle promotes people to their level to incompetence, where they stop. In the Dilbert Principle, it actually intentional. Put them in a role that does the least harm. Keep in mind that the Dilbert Principle is Of course, you also have DEI-based promotions, where it seems like they are simply trying to destroy all organizations.

Question: What are some signs that indicate that a car's alternator has failed? How can we know that our car's alternator has failed before it stops working completely?
Answer: Older cars used to have a voltmeter, a car battery is approximately 12 volts when charged, but the charging voltage is around 13.8 volts. I had an alternator once fail while on a return trip from my parents' home. I noted my car radio display acting odd, and realized my voltage was dropping. I purchased a new battery that got me another 3 hours down the road, close enough where my wife could pick me up (if I recall I swapped car batteries and made it to within 30 minutes, so I just came back later. with a fully charged battery). My point here is that car have way more electronics than a 1987 Dodge Omni, and so your drain would be faster, and you would see all sorts of problems until the car stopped running. Someone else already mentioned that the car would be harder to start (less voltage in the battery). I also noted some issues with a loose alternator or serpentine belt, especially the battery not fully charging. The alternator slips underload, so it does not supply the current required to charge (it essentially becomes a trickle charger).

Question: What should you do to make sure you leave your job on good terms?
Answer: First, that precludes getting yourself fired! Second, give them ample written notice within the terms that are within your company's guidelines. You knew these when you were hired, so they should not be a burden. Now, if you have any sort of office job (that is not rote) then spend you notice period wrapping up any open projects that you can and provide a written pass-on for those that can be closed. Make sure any tool and equipment get turned in. Turn in anything not needed for daily use as soon as possible, and also clean out your personal space and take everything home. Last, do what you can to share some of the more valuable lessons to your remaining team. I am going to assume you like your coworkers, so leave them in as good a shape as possible. Bring in some treats! And where I work, on someone last day we tended to take them out for lunch, and they usually do home right afterward. If your company does not do that, then go out to lunch with several coworkers you were close to over the notice period. Keep everything positive! The fact you want to leave on good terms generally implies you found a better paying job, or something closer to home (I lost two coworkers that had an hour commute because they found a closer job). So don't ruin it with negativity. I presume that even if it was a toxic workplace, some of your coworkers were also “victims” so don't make it harder on them. You could end up their exit strategy if you hear of any openings at your new place. Or five years later, they could be interviewing you when you want to move up again. You never know who you cross paths with again! Ironically the image was from an Harvard article on avoiding shaking hands.

The major complaint with biomedical engineering is it lacks “depth” as you are covering so much material, you never do a deep dive into any single area. Second is mechatronics. It is also a relatively “new” field that combines mechanical, electrical, and computer control systems into one discipline. Though mechatronics has some of the same risks as biomedical (being broad) its main focus is on automation, where the various skills are needed at a systems-level. Everything from industrial robotics and vision systems, to autonomous cars and drones all fall under this discipline.

Question: Why don't engineers unionize?
Answer: Please note it's important to remind my dear readers that this is both US-centric, and focused on engineering as a profession (i.e., four years of college!) This has been covered before by a number of other answers, but I thought I would add to the topic a few points of my own. As most know, airline pilots are also unionized, so it's not exactly out of the question. My point to start out with is that unions are not limited to semi-skilled labor. That said, there are several things wrong with unionizing engineers. First, are rigid pay scales, simply based on time with the company. Not overall industry experience, but time with the company you work for. Now, there might be ways of addressing that. But it would still be a potential can of worms every single time someone with experience is hired. Second, promotions are based on seniority in most unions. I worked in high school as a janitor in a unionized facility, when an opening occurred (retirement, or moved to another company) the open position was bid on. Your time with the company was pretty much the only qualification you needed. Three: unionized facilities also have rigid work rules, of what you can and can't do. Quote frankly, this is my biggest issue with unions in the first place, as I have worn every possible hat with the company I presently work with. If someone lacks a skill, I jump right in and unclog the blockage. Four: They protect underperforming coworkers. Now, that not a huge issue with engineers, but people who don't pull their weight need to be addressed, as the rest of us are going their job. I only had one epically lazy coworker with an engineering background (literally a Wally) as people who are inherently lazy are weeded out in college. Five: Then there is the whole question of union dues. Not just paying someone else a cut of your pay (feel like pay protection money to the mod) but some of its used to find politicians. Finally, keep in mind that engineers are among the highest paid workers in any normal business. In some cases, a senior engineer makes more than a rank & file attorney (the “big law” lawyers seen on TV make up some 10% of the profession). Medical Doctors make more of course, but because of the time in school vs the time working as well as the cost of 4 more years in medical school, doctors don't pass an engineer’s net worth until their 40’s. As long as engineers are in demand, the need to unionize is way below their radars. If you are in a company that doesn't treat their professionals well, then they just move on to somewhere else. After all, engineers also have among the lowest unemployment & underemployment rates among professionals (only teachers and nurses do better overall) The TLDR point: unions are a solution to a problem that does not yet exist. Question: Do you agree that "the people that learn how to use new technology tend to thrive, and the people who don’t tend to stumble"?
Answer: I would say to that yes, in the larger scheme. Of course this is in context to our careers, as in our personal live it does not matter much. So, I was there for the evolution of TV-related technology, but in most cases, people are better off reading a book. Now, lets contrast that to computer technology, as it was a parallel in many ways, with one big difference. When “home” or personal computer first came out, they were quite limited. Not much power (some of the earliest computers had as little as 4k of memory out of the box, so to be useful they need to have their memory upgraded. But the Commodore 64 came out in 1982, so we now have “plenty” of memory. The first killer Apps for such computers were Word Processors and Spreadsheets. Students who used word processors had a leg up over those who had to type (spell check!) and even more so for businesses who were early adopters of computers. I was in the USAF in the 80’s (all of them) and our “shop” got its first computer in 1988. I even learned how to print various forms! Those who embraced this new technology were faster and more productive than those who clung to the old methods. But wait, there’s more! In the 80’s computer advances focused on speed and memory. Computers were still more or less stand alone, but programs also kept being improved. CD-ROM technology came out, and it improved distribution as well as made large databases possible. But the next game changer was networks. Linking all your computers together allowed for internal email, and the sharing of resources like network drive or printers. The internet went a step further. The company I work for in 1998 (the year I was hired) had a single PC in the front office, with dial-up! I requested our IT department connect it to our internal network, and I now had the internet at my desk! However, I still had to go to the office and get online. In less than 6 months, we got a T1 connection! Talk about blazing speeds! Now, we could visit other companies' websites! The information superhighway was here! Our website from a contracted single page to something interactive. And we could email our customers & suppliers. Yes, using the phone is still useful even today, but email does create a record for future reference, and of course documents could be attached. In in the PC world itself, we ended up with 3D modeling (I can't say just how much of a game changer that because for designers) accompanied with CAM software (generating tool paths) and the related development of 3D printing (additive manufacturing) If your office is using paper memos and conventional drafting, you don't exist as a company anymore. Technology moves alone, and if you don't keep up you fall behind. That said, we will see some dead-end technology developments. Bubble memory had promise in the early 80’s but was supplanted by improvements in conventional hard drive technology (the technology S-Curve in action!) Note, in the technology lifecycle curve, the risks are largely in the Innovation phase, though “early adopters” can also be burned at time. So, there are some minor risks there, but it is largely mitigated if you are among the first of the early majority. In my computer example, one IBM entered the desktop PC market, it was pretty much a safe bet. But some places still dont get the memo.

Question: Why do some people think that any problem can be solved by sheer hard work when it's obviously not true?
Answer: Because the implication is that you are also working on the right problem, with the right tools. Now, there are some categories of “Wicked problems” that are near impossible to solve (such as when a solution causes new problems, as when welfare in the US help create an underclass) But let's stick to problems that most of us encounter in our personal or professional lives. The number one issue I found with problems solving at work is people tend to solve the wrong problem. One helpful book that covered this was Double Your Profits: Plug The Leaks In Your Cash flow by Jay Arthur. Two of the basic tools he recommended are simple histograms, and a pareto analysis. Other tools include: Keep in mind that sometimes you will initially start out with a belief that something is the reason for an issue, and after some analysis, you find that you are going in the wrong direction. That is ok, just reassess your data, and redirect your efforts. Troubleshooting issues includes a degree of trial and error (divide and conquer) as often is very important to determine that is not related to the problem. Eliminating as much as possible early on helps to focus your effort in a much smaller area of possible root causes. Now, so far we discussed working smarter vs working harder. So where does working hard tie into this (remember this in the context of solving problems) Because, at the end of the day, you still have to do the work. In most cases, the more data, the better. Some who is lazy or takes shortcuts is simply going to be less effective unless they really get lucky. And guessing answers works once in awhile, but is not the key to long term success. One final aspect: some people quit early, then a problem seems too hard. Its almost like they are afraid of success, so they snatch defeat out of the jaw of victory. And while being mindful of the “sunk cost” fallacy, quitting early (ie, not working hard) has a 100% success rate in not solving problems.

Question: Do people who earn millions per year pay less taxes than those who earn hundreds of thousands per year? Is this considered fair?

Question: I have an e-bike that’s 48V, 2,000 watts. Can I put a swap the current battery and controller for a 72V battery and a controller for more top speed?
Answer: While most electrical devices have a safety margin, its typically around 20-30%. This means that a device designed to operate at a certain voltage or current will be rated for 20-30% higher than its maximum expected operating conditions. The reason why in this case is that the motor is designed for a certain amount of mechanical force at a particular voltage, as well as an RPM. It is also designed for heat dissipation based on its maximum power input, so if we apply nearly twice the voltage, even if it creates no other damage, it will quickly overheat. Now, 72 volts in a 48-volt system is not quite doubling the voltage, it could also exceed the voltage rating of any internal components, especially electrolytic capacitors (provided it was a brushless motor, and had some integrated electronics) Note a 2000 watt electric motor on a eBike is already quite powerful. Question: What are the benefits of having both a PhD in engineering and an MBA?
Answer: This is one of these “it really depends” answers! First, the MBA will set you up for a management track. Many engineers go on to earn one. That said, I seem many people recommend that you earn a MBA later, after working at least 10 years as an engineer. The reason for that is 1) 24-year-olds are NOT ready for leadership positions, even if daddy own the company and 2) by the time you are ready to lead, you have flushed a lot of what you have learned. Second, the PhD is a different animal. In some case it can hurt finding a rank-and-file engineering positions, as evidence shows that a Master’s in Engineering is the sweet spot for most engineer's careers. On the other hand, while earning a MBA by going to night school is fairly common and easy, earning a PhD takes a lot of commitment, and is best done when you are young and are willing to eat Raman noodles for several years. And while we are taking about the benefits, the process is also important. Nevertheless, a PhD in certain areas is of great benefit, as lots of large companies perform R&D. Now, we are speaking of engineering, not computer science (where AI research now is hot) but of course in the modern world there is lots of overlap in the various fields. And while there is a demand for PhDs, the job market is significantly smaller. Now, what about both? In some technology drive companies that could be a ticket to eventually earning a senior management role. And it also gives some credibility to startups seeking investment if one of the founders covers these bases (as one person, or divide up among the team) But remember that credential collection does not guarantee any future success. You could be well educated but have no common sense, especially outside the relatively safe academic world. I’m not suggesting you go either way. I dropped out of grad school, but otherwise did just fine. Oh, look, a comic about PhD’s!

Question: What are the reasons for the decline in modern propeller planes? What advantages do they have over jets?
Answer: First you need to define which market segment where we see the decline in modern propeller planes. Jet aircraft largely took over the commercial airline market in the 1960’s. Some advantage of propeller-based airfraft include… The Lockheed Constellation was considered one of the last great propeller airliners. The DC-7 was the last douglas propeller airliner was well… A design for a large-body airliner based on the B-36 (Convair Model 37) never got past beyond the conceptual stage, though a single XC-99 cargo version was built. Also note that the Lockheed Electra was considered a commercial failure. It was a turboprop, so it was more fuel efficient than a piston engine poweredaircraft, but it could not complete with the first generation Boeing and Douglas airliners (707, DC-8). It also had more design flaws than the Comet, and had a dismal safety record. Despite its failings, the P-3 Orion had greater success as a US Navy aircraft in a ASW role (much like the Comet did in RAF and RN service) The issues with prop-based aircraft were numerous, as larger aircraft engines were heavier and were not that fuel efficient (for the record, nor were the early turbojet engines) but also had limited power and airspeed. Once practical turbojets were available, the market quickly shifted in the 60’s to jet powered aircraft. Advantages of jet aircraft include… Dash 80 in flight But that’s not the entire picture, as turboprops sort of fill in the niche between the propeller vs jet debate… The C-130, one of the most famous of military transports… And the Dash-8, a fairly common small commuter aircraft. So, in smaller market segments where we have turboprops dominate, otherwise jet aircraft simply had too many advantages over propeller aircraft. Now, in general aviation, the opposite is true. It very rare to see a jet-powered private aircraft. In fact, the Cessna 172 is considered the most successful aircraft in history! Over 44,000 have been built, and it is still in production (since 1956!)

Question: If you were alive before the year 2000, you realize how quickly technology has changed. Do you think we’re moving too fast?
Answer: To begin like a number of other answers, I turned 42 in 2002, so I completely witnessed the development & growth of today’s technology. I even got to witness so dead ends that initially showed so much progress, such as bubble memory. Moreover, I was also of the age where some items I worked with were cutting edge, others were throwback to an earlier generation (such as magnetic core memory, and paper tape for loading programs). Again, as one answer pointed out, once personal or home computers were invented in the late 70’s (Apple II, Commodore PET, TRS-80) it simple became faster & cheaper. The Intel 8080 was launched in 1974, and the 8086 launched in 1978. By the end of the 80’s we had the 80486 processor. Early 8-bit computers were limited to 64k, but many came out with 16k and needed to be upgraded. By the end of the 80’s I purchased a PC compatible with 512k. Here is my person experience with computers… But computers were not the only area progress took place. VCRs became a thing in the 80’s, and my first was a top loading version that survived into the mid-90’s. Not only could you time shift your TV watching, but you could also rent movies, and Blockbuster became a thing. Modern streaming is just an evolution of that ability in the sense that prior generation could not do that, though TV station had video tape technology since the 60’s. Just remember that the internet was a late 60’s idea, but was limited to the government & research institutions throughout the 80’s. The decision to open it up allowed the World Wide Web to become a real thing, though you did have commercial dialup services such a Compuserve. the biggest issue with them is they were essential silos, so if you and a friend had different services, you could not talk to each other. I was expecting fixing that to lay the groundwork for the “internet” but it did not happen that way. Some changes were literally under the hood. Cars went from carburetors w/points in the ignition system to throttle-body injection and electronic ignition. The reliability of modern cars has grown tremendously over the years! The largest changes have been in portable devices. We had pocket computers in the 80’s, but it was the Palm Pilot that created the form-factor that even modern smartphones use. The original Palm Pilot was introduced in 1997, and I purchased my Palm IIIxe in the early 2000’s. With their desktop software, I could download my Outlook email & calendar. Now for the question: has technology moved too fast? The advances in aerospace (SpaceX) or with the adoption of solar has not occurred fast enough in my opinion. Now, there is some concern with e-waste with the continued develop of new products with more features. How many of us have ditched perfectly good phones because the latest version has come out? The tech industry is responsible for 2–3% of our carbon emissions. Some larger culprits like bitcoin mining and larger server farms are already under fire. But this is a not moving too fast issue as far as the question is concerned… The real issues are the social changes taking place… So, is technology moving too fast? It going to really be a case-by case basis, and for now the jury is still out.

Question: Why does an aircraft fly at 36,000 feet? Why does the aircraft retract the landing as soon as they take off?

Matthew Sellers is credited with inventing the retractable landing gear (patented it in 1911) and its first application seems Glen Curtiss' Triad airplane in 1911 (the aircraft was amphibious, so it kept the landing gear out of the water!) The first naval fighter aircraft didn't have retractable landing gear until the Grumman FF (1931) The reason is fairly obvious: landing gear adds drag. You want to reduce it as much as possible, especially during take-off. How much? Not this replay from stack exchange: Now to address the attitude portion of the question. Its actually quite simple, as air is thinner at higher attitudes, and related to the earlier landing gear question, its less drag at higher attitudes. So we have a trade-off of drag vs enough air to generate lift (and to a degree, to provide enough air for your powerplant and to operate control surfaces). Question: What steps can one take to become a successful engineering manager without prior experience managing engineers? How does one transition from being an individual contributor to a managerial role in engineering?
Answer: One point to keep in mind is that managing people is very different than engineering. Managing is a skill than need to be learned, as well as leadership (I see each as related, though different). In other words, being a gifted engineer will not necessarily make you a good manager, as the Peter Principle comes to play, for the earlier reason given. But keep this in mind: Managing engineers and technicians is easier than just managing a more random/diverse group of employees, as engineers tend to have the same educational background. So that will work in your favor… But despite the higher (and harder) education that engineers have, just being promoted to a management position had be difficult for both the new manager as well as the people under them. Now, there are things you could do if you find yourself in this position. First, grab a copy of the “One Minute Manager.” Now, it’s not a management degree in a book, but it does have a few timeless principles that can help you deal with your new department. You could also take a few night courses. Most community college have business management courses you could take, just remember that you are not looking to earn a degree! That is the nuts and bolts of management (leading people). Also research “soft skills” and see where you can improve. But as an engineering manager, you also need to learn to think “strategically.” First, two books I recommend to everyone: Both of these books helped me to think differently. Wharton Business School also has a two-course program on Strategic Management on edX. Also remember that unless you are a working manager (common in small companies) your role as a manager is to help your team succeed. In some cases you help them solve problems, by talking it out, helping them form a plan, sharing an experience, or directing a few next steps. So, you still get to use your knowledge, but more in a sharing/mentoring fashion. At other times, you try to get the right people all in the same room! Moving up has its challenges, but it also has its rewards. Have fun!

Question: What are some things that people don't know before getting into engineering?

On the design side, creativity require the application of everything you know. You often take many existing ideas and apply them in new ways. The progress of technology is often just millions of little improvements everywhere. Problem solving is more of the same. But troubleshooting also requires an eye for details, as it can be a very small thing that is keeping something from working. In a prototype, it could be just one bad connection on a prototype. Imagine trying to find the wire you ran to the wring pin! One interesting thing is that learning to code helps develop the logical think process. Anyone who codes at any level know that a good portion of coding is debugging your own code to see where the missing colon is! Or the wrong variable being referenced. Or a million other potential mistakes. The next broad category is just how clueless the rest of the organization is about engineering. Some will think what you do is magic, and the other half something that anyone could do. And to the seconds groups point, I could teach you how to do many of our tasks. You will do well up to the point where you have your first problem. In fact, one thing you will learn is how much the organization will depend on you! No pressure, but if the engineering staff all dies from food poisoning because they all went out together for lunch, the company would grind to a halt in just a few days. The company I work with has recently split into a sustaining group, and a new product development group. The sustaining group will of course focus on daily “fires” but also your process improvement efforts (Lean Six Sigma projects). That will address the issue of “owning” a product line the entire time you are with the company, and then losing the expertise if you leave.

Question: Are general requirements in college a waste of time? What are these requirements there for? Why is it necessary for a software engineer to know about music theory, or a journalist to know about electricity and magnetism?
Answer: There is a lot of various opinions about this, but it really depends on how far the general requirements go, especially for STEM majors. Now, I really enjoyed general education requirements, as in many cases they were 1) an easy “A” and 2) had gender balance (important to 20-year-old males). But when done correctly (as in requiring a term or research paper) you learned to research and organize ideas, and to present compelling arguments. In fact, one of the most valuable classes I took in college was Public Speaking (in my first engineering job, during ECO review meeting you had to present your proposed changes to a room of engineering & managers). Now, I have never seen music theory to be a required course for engineers. I had English composition, American History & Western Civilization, as well as Intro to Psychology, Public Speaking, and one language course. Of course, as a STEM student I had the whole math & science tracks. My AAS program also required 6 hours of management courses, as most people do progress to a supervisor or lead person at some point in their career. Nor have I seen anything beyond a general “survey of Physics” required for non-STEM majors, even though journalists could very well find themselves writing about science & technology-related subjects (and perhaps full-time) My issue is not that we have general education requirements, but it can be overdone. I heard of some cases where engineering students had to take a “gender studies” course, but that was largely done to ensure that dept received “support” (and what better way than to force other students to take such courses?) I work for our local community college with their mechatronics program, and I was surprised how few general education courses were required for that degree (as compared to my CCAF degree in Avionics System Technology, which when counting math was nearly 50% general education). So, not a waste of time if done right. Here is a link I found when searching for an image, it might provide useful tips! Also found this… (Image: Wayne State University)

Question: What are some factors to consider when deciding to drop out of college or university due to failing grades or other issues? What steps should be taken if this decision is made?
Answer: The steps would be to first determine why you are dropping out of school, as each reason would have a different response. If dropping out of school is due to grades, then you need to focus on the root cause. In this case you should never leave this to the last minute, but yet may with into its too late to do something. Later, when taking Calculus (I, II, & III) as well a differential equation's I attended all of the study groups the class created (both formal & informal). In a few cases I also made use of the instructor's office hours. Also, don't be afraid to ask question. You should never leave a class for that day without fully understanding the material. That said, in a few cases a student has simply enrolled in a program that they just can't do. At some point, extra tutoring & study is not going to cut it. At least in the time frame allowed (engineering in particular had been described as “drinking from a fire hose”) Summary here: Now, what about other issues? Some people run out of money. That is unfortunate, but sadly many people overlook going to a community college first. Now, I understand that some states are better than others with transfer of credits, but in most cases you need to pick a program with transferring in mind. Moreover, earning an associate's degree leave you with a credential vs having nothing but some college on your resume. Also, people do forget about the night school option. If you drop out of college (defined as going full-time). If you must quit school, you could still finish your degree as a part-time student. It a longer path (it took me 10 years) but I was also active-duty USAF who had to move several times. But 100% of my education was done as a part-time student, so don't discount that. Finally, if you are deciding to drop out because you interests have changed, then your only consideration is the dent you now carry. If you use a community college first, and quit in your first year, then not much time, money or effort was lost. Even if tuition was “free” to the student, someone had to pay it for you. And worse yet, you might have bumped someone else for the slot.\ Quitting in your fourth year is another story. Sort of snatching defeat from the jaws of victory so of thing. After all, completing a degree tells future employers that you can stick to a long-term project. Quitting at the end say otherwise, that you would walk away if you lost interest. So many things to consider here. The only thing I didn't address here is a health crisis, because they are unique to the individual. All I can say here is to work with the college’s administrative staff to work out whatever options you have. Note the number one reason here… and things like job loss would most affect part-time students (such as myself who received tuition-assistance) Some of these parallel each other, but it also seems like different question were asked.

Question: When a capacitor receives a sudden change in voltage, what happens to its current?
Answer: Remember when an applied voltage to a capacitor is constant, then the current through the capacitor is zero (of course, you might have a miniscule current from internal insulation resistance) The faster the voltage change, the higher the current. Note this simple power supply… When you first turn it on, you have zero volts across C1, but you immediately apply 12 volts. You would see your maximum current through C1, largely limited by the internal resistance from T1 and your diodes (D1-D4) in the bridge circuit. Something similar occurs to C2, except R1 also provides some protection from overcurrent when first turned on. Nevertheless, if an additional load is attached, you might see a drop in voltage which means C2, and to some degree, C1 when then provide more current. But back to the original question, the answer is simply the faster the voltage changes, the higher the current we see in a capacitor.

Question: What contributed to the rise of the personal computer?
Answer: Several things were needed for the “rise” of personal computers. The invention of the microprocessor was vital, and probably goes without saying. The advent of relatively low-cost microprocessors made “home computers” possible. Closely related were low-cost memory chips. And while I like more conventional static RAM, it was dynamic RAM that made memory cheap. Nevertheless, early computers had very limited amounts of memory. In the early 80, it was not uncommon for a computer to have 16k of RAM, with upgrades available for (way) more money. That was one reason why the commodore 64 was such a big hit. The biggest problem between early computers was lack of compatibility. Each manufacturer had their own OS, and even worse, often different formats for floppy disks. So, you could not, for example, work on a document at home on your C64 and take it to work and read the disk on an IBM PC. Because of this, I bought my first MS-DOS machine in 1989 ($1200 for a single floppy “Laser Compact XT” with 512k of ram. I later upgraded it to 640k and figured out how to make a floppy extension cable so I would have a B drive! Keep in mind that MS-DOS and the IBM architecture created a “safe, conservative” environment for business users. The development of VisiCalc and work processers (WordStar) make the PC important to the office at work. There was even a early PC-version of AutoCAD (one of my professors even said he got a math coprocessor, which was also a thing). People don't think about this much, but the lowly dot matrix printer also was an important factor in the adoption of PC’s. It enabled the PC to replace the typewriter in the office, but also make computers useful for students (using word processors to write papers). I was one of them who went through that transition from typing papers to writing them using a word process (I used “Easy Writer” because it was cheap! It really was a game changer! The irony is many printers used the standard Centronics interface, or the RS-232 serial port. It was displaced in the late 90’s and early 2000s by USB, but unlike the floppy issue, there were fewer compatibility issues. I already alluded to software like WordStar and VisiCalc, but one can't overlook the fact that having commercial software that made a computer actually useful for most users was also vital to adopting a personal computer. Most people objection back them was “what am I going to use a computer for” and such software . The irony is very few people used then for storing recipes or creating “databases” for their stamp collection. Games were also a contributor, but dedicated game machine did the job better for many years. And while modems allowed users to connect to BBS systems, the world wide web is probably the tipping point for universal adoption. Web applications like shopping gave most people a reason to have a computer, hence the faster adoption rates in the late 90’s. It also gave rise to instant messaging & social media. Hence, you reading this answer. Been there, done that!

Question: How can we make scientists and engineers as effective now, as they were in the period between 1865 and 1965? Meaningful progress in the last sixty years is rather thin on the ground!
Answer: Look, between 1865 & 1965 we had some of the most fundamental discovers made. And here's the thing: the low-hanging fruit was by then already invented, or discovered. Once you invent the transistor, it's never going to be invented again (unless we have a nuclear war that puts us back to the stone ages). Now, you might create a better version, as we always have people trying to make things better. Still, it one thing to make something existing better, or come up with a improved replacement. Its quite another to come up with an original idea for something that never existed or was done before. The problem is that it is harder for an individual to make fundamental discoveries like we did in the late 1800’s through early 1900’s. Plus, today we often work on teams, and the entry requirements' are higher in many ways. You are often not taken seriously if you lack certain credentials. Being right doesn't matter. And in some fields, there is a lot of resistance to change. Peer review is important, and yet it can also stifle mavericks that could change things radically. But the questions' thesis is that post-1965 engineers & scientists have not pulled their weight, and if you believe that, consider just a few things… So, while we may never see anything like Einstein's 1905 “annus mirabilis” (miracle year), I still expect many amazing inventions and discover to be made. Just look at that CERN or the JWST are able to discover. Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, National Ignition Facility (NIF)

Question: How can an introvert succeed in their career without having friends at work and avoiding office politics?
Answer: Here is a definition from Healthline: Being introverted has to do with how you gather energy. You might be introverted if you’re energized by solo time and feel drained after prolonged social interactions. This isn’t necessarily the same as shyness. Now, I’m fairly shy and a bit introverted. Every weekend I try to walk or bike one of our local greenways. That does not mean that I don't have friends or like social activities, though I do prefer smaller groups. The same is true at work. I have a few work friends that I enjoy working with. Smaller meetings are just fine. In fact, for me the magic number is between 12–20 when I start seeing it was an audience vs a small group. So, for the first half of your question, try to develop some one-on-one relationships. No matter what career you have, you need to interact with others. As for careers, you already know that some are better than others as far as social interaction. Nursing or teaching are of course “social” whereas engineering, programming and other such STEM careers require a lot of “alone time” to do deep dives into your tasks. But that is also employer specific. Home care nurses work one-on-one for example. As do Physical Therapists. In contrast, some engineers work on the production floor as opposed to being alone in a cube. Electricians and plumbers that make house calls typically work alone. But on a construction site, it more of a team. I once worked for the Va State Police was a communications tech, I was on the road a lot in my own vehicle. Minimal interaction. Now, as for the office politics, that's best avoided even if you are an extrovert! Nevertheless, being an introvert make the office politics harder in the sense you don't have a network of support. A lot of office politics involves gossip & rumors, and you don't have that network. So, as you allude to, don't play their game. The is what I found helps… But keep in mind these are “self-preservation” tactics, not for getting ahead by gutting your opponents!

Question: Why do people say the Air Force is lazy?
Answer: Because Lazy is relative. Yes, the physical fitness requirements are lower than the Army or USMC, but the USAF had a different mission. Yes, the other branches work long hours, but I had made share of 12-hours shifts during exercises. But being on duty longer does not mean you are doing physical work. Moreover, if you are working 12-hours a day does not take from someone else also working hard. Working less hours is not working no hours. And yes, very few Airforce members have to dig foxholes. But the Navy does not either! Yes, I get the USAF has better accommodations, and better working conditions. Yet the flightline did amplify the weather: when it was cold, it's really cold! Not all Maintenace was done in hangers after all, and the hardened shelters may have kept you out of the rain, they were not heated. So, in a relative sense the USAF is the least physically demanding of all the branches of the military, though the title “chair force” might shift to the Space Forces. Question: Was an anti-radar version of McDonnell Douglas' F-4 Phantom ever built for the United States Air Force or Navy?
Answer: Only the USAF had a dedicated SEAD version of the F-4. The most famous was the F-4G “wild Weasel” aircraft. It was a modified F-4E, with the gun removed and replaced with the APR-38/47. The APR-38 not only located and identified various threats, it also interfaced with the F-4’s avionics through a “nav coupler” black box. Here is a 1981 photo of an F-4G from George AFB. The only time the F-4G was used in combat was during the 1991 Gulf War. The was also an earlier version, based on the F-4C model. Only a small number were modified, adding the APR 25/26 and ER-142. There were a limited number of conversions, and they flew during the Vietnam war. Of course, there are other EW aircraft. The USAF had an EF-111, and the US Navy had EA-6B Prowlers followed by the current EA-18G (the Movie Maverick should have featured some G-models), but the answers was specific about F-4’s. Question: What are the differences between the army and air force in terms of quality of life, benefits, salary and career opportunities?
Answer: First, your pay and benefits are controlled by congress, not the branches. An E-5 is an E-5 no matter what branch you serve in. Here is the enlisted pay scale from Military(.com). Note there is no branch of service indicated. And the same is true with BAQ/BAS and other allowances. So formal pay & benefits are the same. The Army used to have faster promotions, especially to E4 & E5. Some of that may be due to the Army in the 80’s had a two-year option. Maybe someone could elaborate, but in 1983–84 it took me 29 weeks as an E3 to make E4 (I know the USMC had a “terminal Lance” thing going on, but they were not part of the question). I was so upset that when I was able to test for E5, I studied like it was a college final. I even took CLEP & DANTES exams as “practice tests” to get me better prepared. It paid off, as I made E5 & E6 on my first attempt. As for career opportunities, there are two ways to view this: while active duty and after you leave the service. I’d assume that within certain career fields, you are going to have similar jobs. The Airforce had helicopters; the army has lots more. Yet the skills & training to maintain them would be similar. That includes avionics, engines (propulsion) and airframe. The largest difference is the Army has a whole bunch of combat careers, whereas the USAF does have a small number of security forces. The army would also have a much larger number of heavy equipment operators. So, while the USAF does have a higher percentage of technical jobs, that’s only a fraction of jobs that are available. The USAF does have a benefit of have its own community college, with each career fields having its own AAS degree. In fact, my first degree was through CCAF, in Avionics Systems Technology. Note this: Finding a job after leaving the military is almost never an easy task. Unless you're transferring into a civilian field that directly relates to your military experience, you will need to change fields in order to enter the civilian workforce (Bryan Wolfe) From BLS: The unemployment rate for veterans who served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces at any time since September 2001—a group referred to as Gulf War-era II veterans—was little changed at 3.3 percent in 2023 and the rate for all veterans was unchanged at 2.8 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. I picked my career based on the length of training, and the fact I was already interested in electronics and also wanted to work on aircraft. I knew these skills transferred, but also knew I wanted to earn a BS degree. You milage might vary, but for now we also have the GI Bill. I served in the 80’s so I was “between” GI bills, so it was essentially tuition assistance or bust. So, I left the USAF with a BS degree. With two kids by then I was not going to be able to go back to school that easily. Finally, about the quality of life. Again, there are several aspects to consider. The USAF is a military branch, it is still military, with lots of borrowed army traditions. The biggest issue with the Army (to me) would be the size of most bases. A typical 80-era fighter wing would have about 5000 airmen. So, you had hundreds of single airmen hitting the bars of the typical “small town” an Air Base would be located in. Many B-52 bases were northern tier (Maine, UP Michigan, the Dakotas) so that had an impact on a young person's social life. My first assignment was in Goldsboro NC, which seemed to be a bit too “small townish” for my liking, even though Raleigh was just an hour's drive away. My second was Clark Air Base was significantly different, to put it mildly. To put that in perspective, Pope AFB was co-located on what was then Fort Bragg, in Fayetteville NC. We nicknamed the town “fayette-nam.” And when I visited Fayetteville to see Ozzy Osborne, the town lived up to its name (nothing bad occurred, just observing everything around me). Take from this what you wish, as we all have different expectations in life. For example, even though the USAF was “better” in many regards, I still found as a 20-year-old plenty to complain about! Imagine that!

Question: What are the differences in quality of life between the US Army and US Air Force? Which branch is considered to have a higher quality of life and why?
Answer: The USAF was considered to have the best quality of life between all branches of the military, and that really stems from three areas… First, the USAF invests a lot of money into facilities. They have better dorms, for example. In the 80’s they were refurbishing the dorms into having semi-private showers (one between every two rooms). Second, the mission was different. Most of the work was aircraft maintenance, with the rest of the base design to support that activity. There is no “being out to sea” or “field maneuvers.” Instead, it was way more 9–5 than any other branch of the military. Thus, it was easier to take off-duty courses. Of course, we still had exercises. And deployments. But we also got a per-diem (food allowance) so when I was deployed to Korea for 6 weeks, we ate dinner almost every night at the NCO club. And showered at the gym. Only the Space Force will have it easier in that regard, as it will truly be a 9–5 job for enlisted. Third, the USAF attracts a higher quality recruit. When I enlisted any drug or alcohol-related infraction prevented you from enlisting. In other words, no record of any kind. Now, this is not to say the other branches did not have high quality people. The Army in the 80’s had a $25,000 army college fund, of which I was tempted to take advantage of. And the Navy’s technical training was just as good or not better than the USAF (the Air Force has a tendency to over-specialize). If you wanted a relatively normal life, the USAF was the best option. New dorm room at Eglin AFB (USAF photo) Edit: I wanted to share one experience that really drives this point home: we were having an annual exercise at Spangdahlem Air base in Germany. How, the base also hosted a US Army Air Defense Battalion, along with our fighter wing. During the exercise, our Comm Squadron set up a satellite facility off base. One of the SP’s that I took classes with was providing security. A routine Army patrol dropped by. Their NCO stepped in the tent, and simply said I can’t let me guys see this… that had a microwave, mini-fridge and a TV with VCR.
