Question: My girlfriend cheated on me after a 4 year relationship. I can't reconcile with the fact that she slept with someone else, considering we had only been with each other before this. Will I be able to forget with time? Do we have a future?
Answer: Whether you have a future depends on her attitude towards that mistake. You have made it clear that you were deeply hurt though. And quite frankly it's your decision to move on or work on the relationship. Don't let anyone try to push you into a decision. It's your pain, deal with it your own way. The pain will lessen with time, but the rate of change is also deeply personal. I didn't date for nearly two years after my 10-year marriage broke up. I didn't even meet my current wife until my ex wife got married. One tip: do find a friend who been there and will listen. If they have some advice or suggestions do consider them, but again make sure it's your decision. When I went through my divorce one of my friends was also going through one as well. We hung out almost every Sunday afternoon and had a pizza while watching a game on TV. It helped a lot (and I don't even like sports!)

Question: How should I (as a girl) treat guys (men/boys)? Because we usually hear about mothers teaching their sons how to treat girls, to be a gentlemen, etc; but barely the opposite. How can they feel valuable?
Answer: In a sense, there are two parts to this question. First, we have the general part of where we treat all people with dignity & respect. If saying something to a girl (woman) is bad, then most likely saying the same thing to a boy (man) is also bad. After all, if we say that girls are “more emotional” than boys, that does not mean that all girl have the same emotion reactions. Heck, I had two daughter and they were as polar opposite as two kids could be. My point here is the most emotionally sensitive boys can very well be more sensitive than the least sensitive girls. And my point here is you dont know where any particular girl or boy might be on the scale. That said, there are some generalizations to consider with boys. Men tend to be a bit more competitive. It does not matter if its sports, or grades, cars, or even girls. guys will compete with each other to see who is the “best.” I had a lot of issues with high school because i thought I was always being ranked in every activity I was involved in (unless with just a few close friends). And most of the time that ranking was only occurring in my head. Though saving face is a big thing in Asian cultures, it also exists in the west. No guy likes to be put down in from of others, but in front of girls (women) is a particularly nasty form of hell. In other words, Boys/men want to be respected. Both by peers, but especially by the opposite sex. So, by showing you recognize that skill or ability that they might have cultivated, it goes a long way to building up their self-esteem. That was probably why my “union job” with adult coworkers was my best memories doing high school. They simply accepted me and treated me as one of the crew at work. So while men may compete with each other, just being in the competration make you feel like a worthy opponent, if that makes sense. By the way, this article help me to make peace with my high school years.

Question: How did you handle failure?
Answer: As we all know, failure is never fun. But keep in mind that how I deal with it really depends on the specific situation. In some cases, I’d just move on. Most failure are not catastrophic, after all. When I was younger, and single, if I asked a girl out and she said “no” than I’d move on and ask someone else. I take the same position at work. If I proposed an idea, and its rejected, I just move on to something else. There are plenty of ideas that will follow. In other words, I don't hang all of my self-esteem on just one event. Now, if the failure is a project, as in the prototype did work, then it became a chance to learn. To do a deep dive and analyze why it failed. And again, a failure or setback of this nature does not derail the entire project. Infact, you want to be agile: fail fast! Then learn all you can't and try again, applying all of the lessons learned. To quote Hannibal Smith: The Opera is not over until the fat lady sings! To expand on this idea here, is don't quit too early. Some people are good at snatching defeat out of the jaws of victory. I’m not one of them. Now, in some cases there is the “sunk cost” fallacy in which you keep pouring time & money into a doomed project. There are times to give up. If that's the case, I just move on. But again, sometimes you learn the most from such failures, so keep that in mind. You can't unlearn something. The IBM “stretch” computer in the early 60’s was a commercial failure, but 80% of its design was used in the System 360 (which is considered one of the most successful products of all time). So, i believe that a single failure is not the end of the world! It can set you up for something better, if you have the right mindset.

Question: Is it OK if I drop out of college?
Answer: Depends on the reason you are quitting college…. If you are quitting because you dont have the “intellectual” ability to complete a degree program, then you are making the smart decision. Now, not everyone is cut out for engineering, or medical school. But some people feel they must have a degree at all costs, so once they drop out of a harder program, they normally find something easier (even if its not their passion). But keep in mind It’s not all or nothing. An applied science (or arts) associates degree or even a trade school that teaches a practical skill is still education. And remember that some fields like psychology have a 40% underemployment rate, which means that completing a degree may not help you find a job that's any better than what a highschool graduate could find (and if the same age, they now have several years experience over you!) If you dropout of college because you dont have interest in any of the types of careers that college graduates tend to work in, dropping may be a good choice. Now, in some cases we have entrepreneurs who quit college after a few years to start a business. You dont need to have a business degree to start your own business, but what you learn in the first few years are the basics. There also also a number of careers that do not require a college degree but do require training: police or fireman, air traffic controller, truck driver. Welders, plumbers and electricians typically have some sort of trade school or community college training. Other construction jobs use “on the job training” (machining is another career that is big into apprenticeships). The issue I see there is if you can't stick to a college program, you also might have trouble with an apprenticeship (though it could be that the classroom was just “not you”) That said, I’m a big fan of getting both skills training along with a general education. There is no sense (in my mind) of arguing for one or the other when you have the both option. But if someone does the 2-year community college option, at least you have a fall-back credential in case you burn out or decide to change gears. This also highlights that role of passion when going to college, as opposed to it being a rite of passage or something that was expected of you. Or even doing it just because you hope for higher earnings. Remember when I said 40% of psychology students dont find jobs that require college degrees? That also means that 60% in fact do so. But guess who is in the 60%? Those with more passion, that worked hard and didn't just see college as a four-year break between highschool and the real world. I heavily lean to option #2.
